user_input: Everyone in our wing is in this unofficial WhatsApp group where they plan weekend trips, late-night tea runs, and valorant matches. Last night I watched them all walk past my door laughing, heading out for a birthday treat, and my room felt like a concrete coffin. I'm literally paying to live in a hostel full of people, yet I've never felt more agonizingly alone.
sandhi_response: Hearing your wingmates walk by while you feel trapped behind your door is a deeply painful kind of isolation, especially when you want so badly to connect. user_input: We had to form groups of four for the DBMS project today, and my heart was literally hammering against my ribs. user_input: I can't even stand up in the DSA lab to ask the TA a basic doubt because I'm terrified the guys next to me will laugh or think I'm stupid for not getting it. Everyone else is cracking off-campus referrals, chatting up seniors, and making networks on LinkedIn, and here I am, choking on my own breath in a room full of people. I feel so utterly cut off from everyone, like there's an invisible glass wall between me and the rest of the batch.
sandhi_response: Your worth as a student and a human being is not defined by how smoothly you can navigate a high-pressure room. user_input: Every evening, my hostel corridor gets so loud with guys planning their weekend trips and talking about their CGPAs. I literally wait inside my room with the lights off, listening through the door, just so I can walk to the washroom without bumping into anyone and having to make awkward small talk. I desperately want to make friends, but whenever someone says a simple 'hi' in the lobby, my throat tightens, I mutter something incoherent, and I walk away fast. They probably think I'm some arrogant snob, but in reality, I'm just incredibly lonely and terrified of messing up the only interaction I might get.
sandhi_response: It is exhausting to live in a state of constant hyper-vigilance, wanting connection so deeply while your body treats it as an active threat. Please be gentle with your silent retreats; protecting yourself from overwhelming anxiety is a survival response, not a personal failure.

user_input: I forced myself to go to the coding club orientation today because my parents keep saying I need to build a 'network' to get a good package. The auditorium was packed, and the seniors were so confident, throwing out jokes and picking people from the crowd to speak. I was sitting near the back, literally praying they wouldn't look at me, with cold sweat running down my back. I couldn't take the noise and the social pressure anymore, so I slipped out the back door halfway through and sat in the empty library staircase crying. I feel like such a failure, I can't even handle a basic college club meet without losing my mind.
sandhi_response: Stepping into a loud, high-expectation environment when you are already feeling disconnected is an enormous hurdle, and choosing to walk out was actually a step of self-preservation, not failure. Let's honor the limits of your energy today and focus on finding small, quiet ways to connect that don't require you to perform.

user_input: My roommate's birthday was last night, and they had this huge cake-smashing thing in the hostel wing with like thirty guys crammed into our room. I sat on my lower bunk, pretending to be deeply engrossed in my notes for the upcoming midterms, feeling completely invisible while everyone laughed and took videos for their Instagram stories. Someone finally asked me why I was being such a buzzkill and not joining in, and I just froze, unable to explain that the noise and the crowd were making my chest collapse. I ended up leaving the room to sleep in the common library, feeling like an absolute alien who doesn't belong anywhere on this campus.
sandhi_response: Sitting in a room full of celebration while feeling completely isolated is a deeply painful experience that can make you feel entirely out of place. It is okay that large, chaotic social rituals aren't your space, and you deserve to find connections that feel peaceful rather than performative.

user_input: Every Friday night is the same torture. There is nothing fundamentally broken in you; your path to connection just requires a gentler, slower pace than the effortless ease you see in others.
